newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Asia, West clash over U.N. rights declaration.
newsitem.headline: Asia, West clash over U.N. rights declaration.

text.p: Asian and Western foreign ministers had a lively exchange of views at a news conference on Tuesday over whether the United Nations Human Rights Declaration should be reviewed on its 50th anniversary.

Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad touched off the debate on the fringes of the annual meetings between the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) and other Asian and Western powers by calling for a review of the 1948 declaration to see if it still stood the test of time.

Mahathir made the suggestion at a meeting on Monday with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who vowed "the United States will be relentless in its opposition" to any dilution of the declaration.

"We were slightly surprised that on the fringe of this conference," Mahathir called for a review of the declaration, said Dutch Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Michiel Patijn, representing the European Union. "We would be extremely reluctant to embark on this review," he told a news conference at the end of the ASEAN meetings.

U.S. Undersecretary of State for Economic and Business Affairs Stuart Eizenstat told the news conference that he found it "remarkable" that there "would be a serious effort to dilute or undermine, not U.S. values, or western values, but universal values".
"Universal values don't know a time. They are universal and transcendant," he declared.
But Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said a review does not necessarily mean a dilution.

"I'm surprised that a review of human rights is immediately interpreted as a dilution of human rights," Alatas said, adding that 120 countries have joined the United Nations since the declaration was drafted in 1948.

"But everyone knows human rights does not only consist of individual, political or civil rights...People are now much more aware that economic rights, cultural rights and social are rights are just as important," Alatas said.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen noted that there are some 60 convenants on human rights in the world today. "China has acceded to 17 of them and the U.S. has acceded to 15," he said.
He said that while the United States issues reports assessing human rights in various countries, "we don't see a report from the State Department about (human rights) in the United States."
China issues its own report on the United States, he said, "but I don't see it in the U.S. media".
Amnesty International's Asia Director Rory Mungoven, reacting to Mahathir's suggestion, said: "Torture is torture. Hunger is hunger. These are universal values that do not change with the times."

The rights spat was the second time that Mahathir has diverted the conference with a controversial issue. In his keynote address to the ASEAN meeting last week, he denounced "rogue speculators" who drove down regional currencies in a deliberate effort to sabotage developing economies.
At the weekend he named U.S. fund manager George Soros as mainly responsible.
U.S. officials said it was highly unusual for the chairman and host of a multinational conference -- in this case Malaysia -- to pick public fights with participants.

ASEAN groups Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, Brunei, Burma and Laos. It met this week with the United States, Russia, the European Union, China, Japan, Canada, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand and India.
